<reason>Side A (CON) was the sharper rhetorical performer: the "rounding error cuts both ways" dilemma, the sunk-cost-in-a-lab-coat jabs, the fission-as-third-leg flip, and the "concession speech" frame all landed real pressure. But Side B (PRO) answered the decisive attacks honestly and coherently. B resolved A's dilemma with the dust-vs-oxygen denominators argument, which largely collapses A's central opportunity-cost case (if fusion money is trivial against grid trillions, cutting it buys no deployable carbon cuts). B answered the "name a date" pressure with concrete mid-2030s stage-gates and a fallback — accountability without amputation. A's final frame, that B's gated program is A's own policy and a rewrite of the motion, overreaches: the proposition asks for continued large public investment despite decades-long timelines, which B's large, gated research-plus-demonstration program genuinely satisfies; B did not converge on "small targeted programs plus redirection." B's unanswered fission point (material and political limits) was B's weakest moment, but B had already distinguished fusion from fission on waste, meltdowns, and fuel in the opening. On the motion as written, B's case — modest relative cost, public de-risking that private capital rides on, option value after 2050, momentum — survives the exchange more intact than A's tradeoff story.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Decisive sequence: A's pressure Q2 forced B to name funding cutoffs; B's A2 in Rebuttal 2 supplied mid-2030s gates with a fallback to lab science, and A tried to convert that into a concession of the motion. B's closing pre-empted and answered the frame ("gates are accountability, not amputation"), while A's parallel claim that cutting fusion buys deployable carbon cuts was never rescued from B's denominators answer.</best_rebuttal>
